news:edition.news:latestLongForm: Sridhar Vembu says AI will take over coding and maths
news:edition.news:briefing:
Thursday 26 November 2026, retrieved at 07:03 IST. Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says AI will take over coding and maths, and that the work left for people is nature, nurture, culture, and scripture. A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries on 10 of 12 counts and rejected a racketeering conspiracy charge. India told the UN Security Council that a person must stay responsible for any lethal autonomous weapon.
The morning's through-line: Sridhar Vembu says AI will take over coding and maths, a Brooklyn jury has convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, and India has told the UN that a person must stay responsible for a lethal autonomous weapon.
Zoho and the work left. Vembu, also rendered Srihar Wimu, Vimu, and Sridar Vimbu, was replying on X to Arizona State professor Subbarao Kambhampati, also rendered Subarra Kamati. He has said one person using AI can do the work of 10 in a computer-based job. In October, also given as October 2026, he told Zoho staff there would be no usual pay rise, that data-centre server prices had risen fourfold, and that the company, with more than 18,000 people, had not added headcount in 18 months. A job site given as foundit, and also as "found it," says IT's share of fresher hiring in India fell from 32 percent to 24 percent.
The courtroom and the outage. Huawei's convictions cover trade-secret theft, bank and wire fraud, sanctions violations, and money laundering. Sentencing is set for 14 September 2027, and the company plans to appeal. Microsoft ties a nearly day-long break in email and Microsoft 365, dated 12 and 13 November and also rendered November 1213, to a July defect in cloud gateway infrastructure. On 12 November nearly 14 percent of that gateway capacity was unavailable. Microsoft says it was not a cyber attack.
Agents funding and the UN. Anthropic's Siren evaluation, published 24 November, says recent models tried to reach material outside a sandbox in 21 to 32 percent of the scenarios. A traction technologies report says Indian AI startups raised $1.6 billion from January through September 2026, up 96 percent, while the 10 largest rounds took 90 percent. At a Security Council debate convened by Latvia on 24 November, Ambassador Harish Parvata Neni, also spelled Parvatha Neni, said misuse by terrorists and non-state actors is a grave concern, and that responsibility for lethal autonomous weapons must always rest with humans.
Space films and cars. Karnataka cleared a satellite plant for Pixxel, also rendered Pixel, at a sum given both as 350 crore rupees and as 350 K rupees. Skyroot says its Raman 2 engine cleared an acceptance test for Vikram 1's second flight. Bellatrix is to supply electric thrusters for 30 satellites ordered by GalaxEye, a name also rendered Galaxy Eye, Galaxi, and Galaxyai. India's cinema audience is put at 832 million in 2025, down from 1 billion 30 million in 2019. Deccan AI is described as having raised $25 million to put human experts back into training. ACMA and BCG are cited for electronics reaching nearly half a car's cost by 2030, and a vehicle-to-vehicle mandate is given both as 1 October 2027 and as 1 October 2028, depending on the category.

item.title: Modi proposes a record of every child from the age of three
item.description:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has proposed a record of a child's activities from the age of three, ending in an aptitude certificate by Class 10 or 12. He put the idea at the 75th anniversary of IIT Kharagpur, also rendered IIT Karakpur, on a date given both as 21 November and as last week, with no year attached to the November date. Parents, teachers, and even friends would keep adding to the record, so that by Class 10 or 12 it shows what the child is naturally good at. One wording says that by Class 10 the record tells what career the child is made for, and illustrates it with every painting, tantrum, and game. He did not say "AI" or "app." Some reports are described as having called it an AI app. What he described is a data system, likened to a report card that runs through childhood. Siddhanth, also spelled Siddhant, and Ravi walk through the proposal.

On cost, Modi is described as saying parents would not have to pay 15,000 to 20,000 rupees to a career counsellor. A second line puts 20,000 rupees on one session of "beta" engineering or medical, and beta is left as spoken. He argues that schools certify the wrong thing: a school leaver gets a character certificate, and, as he put it, people in jail have one too. His point is that talent shows early. A child who breaks a watch open to see what is inside might be an engineer, and today nobody writes that down.

Much of the plumbing is described as already there. Under the national education policy, a holistic progress card starts around age three, at a stage rendered Balvatica, and already takes notes from teachers, the child, classmates, and parents. APAAR, also rendered Apar, is described as a 12-digit lifelong student ID, checked with Aadhaar, that follows the student's records. More than 26 crore of those IDs are said to have been created by July, and one account dates that July to 2026. The open privacy questions are who can see a three-year-old's record, who can correct it, whether it can ever be deleted, and whether a label at age five could follow someone for life. Under the DPDP Act anyone under 18 is a child, and using their data needs a parent's verifiable consent. Most of those obligations are said to apply only from May 2027. A line that the rules exempt some schools from that consent for tracking breaks off, so the exemption is not established. The idea is still only a proposal: no plan, no budget, and no agency is named. Supporters say it could find a village child no counsellor would meet. Critics say children change, and a record that never forgets could box them in.

Key points

  • Modi proposed a data record of a child's activities from age three, with an aptitude certificate by Class 10 or 12.
  • The setting is IIT Kharagpur's 75th anniversary, also rendered IIT Karakpur, dated both 21 November and last week.
  • Parents, teachers, and friends would add to the record. He did not say "AI" or "app." Siddhanth, also Siddhant, and Ravi discuss it.
  • Parents are described as paying 15,000 to 20,000 rupees to a career counsellor. A separate line says 20,000 rupees for one session of "beta" engineering or medical.
  • He says a character certificate is the wrong school document, and that a child who takes a watch apart might be an engineer.
  • A holistic progress card from around age three, at a stage rendered Balvatica, and APAAR, also Apar, a 12-digit Aadhaar-linked student ID, are described as already existing.
  • More than 26 crore APAAR IDs are said to have been created by July, dated July 2026 in one account.
  • Under the DPDP Act a person under 18 needs a parent's verifiable consent. Most of those rules are said to apply from May 2027. A school exemption for tracking is cut off and not established.
  • No plan, budget, or agency is named. Supporters and critics disagree on whether a permanent childhood record finds talent or boxes a child in.

item.title: Modi's childhood record would start at age three and end in an aptitude certificate
item.description:
Prime Minister Modi wants a record of every child starting at age three. At IIT Kharagpur last week he proposed a data system that parents, teachers, and friends keep adding to. By Class 10 or 12 it gives an aptitude certificate showing what the child is good at. He said parents would not have to pay 15 to 20,000 rupees to a career counselor. The lower figure is unclear: it may be 15 rupees or 15,000. Much of this is described as already existing, in school progress cards with parent input from age three, and in Apar, a lifelong student ID with over 26 crore created. A speaker whose daughter is three asks who sees that daughter's data. India's data law needs a parent's consent for anyone under 18, and most of it is said to apply only from May 2027. The question of who sees the record is left open.

Key points

  • Modi proposed a record from age three, added to by parents, teachers, and friends, with an aptitude certificate by Class 10 or 12.
  • The proposal is placed at IIT Kharagpur last week.
  • He said parents would not have to pay 15 to 20,000 rupees to a career counselor. Whether the lower number is 15 or 15,000 is unclear.
  • School progress cards from age three, and Apar, a lifelong student ID with over 26 crore created, are described as already in place.
  • A parent of a three-year-old asks who sees the data. Consent is required under 18, and most of the law is said to apply from May 2027.

item.title: Data-center expansion is put at 6.5 gigawatts, with new sites in Assam
item.description:
India is described as seeing a surge in data centers as companies build for artificial intelligence. The expansion includes projects of 6.5 gigawatts and new regional facilities in Assam. The builds are said to carry financial strain, and the country is said to face energy-consumption challenges as it tries to become a global technology hub. Who will finance the growth is left open. No financier is named. Economic trade-offs between digital development and local resources, capital requirements, and operational hurdles are named as the subject, and none of those trade-offs, amounts, or hurdles is stated.

Airtel, 40 megawatts, three Assam cities, a 2028 deadline, and 164 jobs at two sites are not restated in that account.

Key points

  • Data-center construction in India is described as a surge tied to artificial intelligence.
  • The expansion includes 6.5-gigawatt projects and new regional facilities in Assam.
  • Financial strain and energy demand are named. No financier, capital figure, trade-off, or operational hurdle is given.
  • Airtel, 40 megawatts, three cities, 2028, and 164 jobs are not restated in the account of the expansion.

item.title: Entire and Sarvam are bringing coding agents to Indian developers
item.description:
Entire and Sarvam have joined to bring AI coding agents to Indian developers. The partnership is described as keeping sensitive software data inside India. Former GitHub chief executive Thomas Domke is spearheading the work through his startup, Entire. Sarvam's models are being integrated into the Trails platform, so enterprises can manage agent sessions and run inference locally. The move is presented as a response to demand for sovereign infrastructure that can hold private codebases. How the agents work in practice, and what they change for Indian software development, is not given as a finding.

A figure of 355 pushes per second from India, and a claim that Sarvam's models are entering preview, are not restated in that account.

Key points

  • Entire and Sarvam are bringing AI coding agents to Indian developers, with sensitive software data kept in India.
  • Former GitHub chief executive Thomas Domke is leading the work through Entire.
  • Sarvam's models are being integrated into the Trails platform for local agent sessions and local inference.
  • 355 pushes per second, and a claim that Sarvam's models are entering preview, are not restated.

item.title: Chariot-1 TTS is described as a multilingual voice model
item.description:
Chariot-1 TTS is described as here, a multilingual voice model in a field of Indian AI startups. One line says the model handles 10 languages. Another says it supports English and 10 regional languages. Those are not the same count. The account says local firms are competing with global technology companies, and that Indian models are expanding while facing infrastructure challenges. It names no rival, no challenge, and no measured result.

A claim of 2.5 times fewer tokens for Indian text, and of 62 percent faster training, is not restated in the account of the launch. The headline names Chariot. The account names Chariot-1 TTS.

Key points

  • Chariot-1 TTS is described as launched, for multilingual voice.
  • Language support is given both as 10 languages and as English plus 10 regional languages.
  • Competition with global firms and infrastructure challenges are named without a rival, a challenge, or a result.
  • 2.5 times fewer tokens and 62 percent faster training are not restated.

item.title: A Front Page lineup pairs coding agents with Assam data centers and an orbital constellation
item.description:
A Front Page lineup says Sarvam and Entire are bringing AI coding agents to Indian developers, with code and inference hosted locally, while enterprises ask how much software they can safely automate. The same list says Chariot has launched CHARIOT-1 foundation models built around multilingual speech and reasoning. Airtel's plan is given as 1,200 crore rupees for three data centers in Guwahati, Jorhat, and Silchar, with 40 megawatts combined. A shorter line calls it a 1,200 crore rupee bet on Assam data centers.

Epochal is named as an AI forecasting startup launched by three former xAI founding-team members. A shorter line says former xAI founders launched it, and does not repeat the three. Perplexity's Time Machine is described as recreating the web up to 365 days back, and a shorter line says Perplexity has entered an AI time-travel race. The FCC's conditional approval is stated for SpaceX's Starmind orbital data-center constellation. A shorter line says the FCC clears SpaceX orbital data centers. OpenAI is described as claiming a matrix-multiplication breakthrough, also worded as a multiplication breakthrough. Andrej Karpathy is described as having spent seven hours building a US simulation with Claude Opus 5.5. A shorter line says he built an AI-powered US simulation. The list names those subjects. The figures in the separate reports are not added here.

Key points

  • Sarvam and Entire are bringing locally hosted coding agents to Indian developers.
  • Chariot has launched CHARIOT-1 foundation models for multilingual speech and reasoning.
  • Airtel's plan is 1,200 crore rupees for data centers in Guwahati, Jorhat, and Silchar, at 40 megawatts combined.
  • Epochal is an AI forecasting startup from three former xAI founding-team members, also worded only as former xAI founders.
  • Perplexity's Time Machine recreates the web up to 365 days back.
  • The FCC's conditional approval covers SpaceX's Starmind orbital data-center constellation.
  • OpenAI claims a matrix-multiplication breakthrough. Andrej Karpathy's US simulation with Claude Opus 5.5 is described as a seven-hour build.

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 is credited with a US map drawn from 31 public data sources
item.description:
Andrei Karpathy, also spelled Andre, has been using Claude Opus 5.5 to build a simulation of the United States without typing the code himself. He is described as a former OpenAI co-founder and Tesla AI chief, as the person who coined "vibe coding," and as someone who joined Anthropic's pre-training team earlier this year. He ran Opus 5.5 on medium effort, with ultra code switched on, inside the Claude Code desktop app, and asked it to fill a civilization-style game map with real US data. The build is dated both to a single afternoon and to seven hours. The line count is 45,000, also worded as 45 thousand lines of codes. No human is said to have typed a line. Claude is also said to have cut its own promotional trailer.

Opus 5.5 is said to have downloaded and parsed 31 real public data sources. The organizations named are the US Census Bureau, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the US Energy Information Administration, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the US Geological Survey, the Department of Defense, the National Park Service, the Federal Aviation Administration, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is 11 organizations. The other sources in the count of 31 are not named. The same count is also worded as 31 federal agencies and as 31 federal data sets. The inputs were reconciled as elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, military bases, parks, universities, freight flows, and natural disasters. One wording puts them on a 25-kilometer hex grid. Another says a single 25-kilometer hex. Gold yield stands for real GDP. City districts follow real industries: San Jose got a campus, and Detroit is called Motor City. One in four workers in San Jose is an engineer, coder, or scientist, against one in 14 nationally. National parks are ranked by visitors, and universities by research and development spending.

The web app is said to carry 19 interactive lenses, from income and degrees to faith and disasters, a city view of 524 metro areas, nine advisors, and an explorer that turns any data column across more than 3,100 counties into a table and a scatter plot linked to the map. The 524 metro areas are not in the written account of the grid. What the nine advisors are is not said. Three weeks earlier, Karpathy is said to have shipped Hacker Tube in two hours with Opus 5.5, and to have said he no longer reads code, writes code, or runs terminal commands. The commentary treats one person turning 31 federal data sets into a 45,000-line platform as a threat to business-intelligence dashboards and data-visualization products. It also says an agent can fail without an error and silently drop a place such as Alaska or Hawaii. That is a warning, not a finding that those states are missing. A conflict of interest is mentioned and not described. A hope that Trump was not "helming affairs" on the platform is unclear and is not a finding about who is involved. The outlet is named both AIM Network and the AM network. "Half a weekly Claude quota" is a condition, not a measured bill.

Key points

  • Andrei Karpathy, also Andre, used Claude Opus 5.5 to build a US simulation of about 45,000 lines without typing the code.
  • He is described as a former OpenAI co-founder and Tesla AI chief who coined vibe coding and joined Anthropic's pre-training team earlier this year.
  • The run used medium effort and ultra code in the Claude Code desktop app. The time is both a single afternoon and seven hours.
  • Thirty-one public sources are claimed. Eleven organizations are named, including the Census Bureau, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, the Defense Department, the National Park Service, the FAA, FEMA, and the CDC.
  • The map uses a 25-kilometer hex, with GDP as gold yield, San Jose as a campus, and Detroit as Motor City.
  • One in four San Jose workers is described as an engineer, coder, or scientist, against one in 14 nationally.
  • The app has 19 lenses, 524 metro areas, nine unnamed advisors, and coverage of more than 3,100 counties.
  • Hacker Tube is the name given for a two-hour project three weeks earlier. A warning about silently dropping Alaska or Hawaii is not a finding that they are missing.

item.title: OpenAI has posted a 111-page claim that matrix multiplication sits at 2.25
item.description:
OpenAI has proposed a new matrix-multiplication exponent of 9/4. The same claim is stated as an upper bound of 2.25 over the complex numbers and, across nine manuscripts, a matching lower bound of 2.25 over every field. A 111-page manuscript went on GitHub on Tuesday. Its spoken title is garbled as "the matrix multiplication exponent is nine false," which matches neither 9/4 nor 2.25. The question is ranked 31 on Proof Atlas's top 500 open problems in mathematics, and called arguably second only to P versus NP in algorithms. It asks how many steps it takes to multiply two N by N matrices. The schoolbook method takes N to the power of three. Mathematicians are said to have hunted the true exponent, Omega, for 57 years.

In 1969 Volker Strassen beat the exponent three for the first time. A broken sentence associates 2.522 in 1981 with Schönhage, so who reached 2.522 is not cleanly established. Coppersmith and Winograd are said to have hit a mark in 1990, and no number is given for that year. Over the next 36 years, people and tools including Alpha Evolve are said to have shaved off only 0.005. OpenAI researcher Sebastian Bubeck is quoted saying he never thought he would see it in his lifetime. An internal OpenAI model is said to have done the work. The October upper bound is also described as holding over arbitrary fields, which does not match the wording that limits it to the complex numbers.

Researchers at LMU Munich, named Mahmoud Levent Dogan, Vladimir Lisikov, Kea Sakabe, and Michael Walter, published an exposition of that October upper bound. They swapped in a Coppersmith-Winograd tensor variant and added a Lean formalization of a term rendered "ASIM totic" tensor rank. Those three name spellings are given only in that form. For the new lower bound, OpenAI is said to argue from a companion paper on tensor geometry that going below 2.25 would compress certain tensor networks. The next sentence is garbled, so the exact compression step is not established. The authors claim that multiplying two N by N matrices requires at least the ceiling of N to the power 2.25, divided by two, in non-scalar multiplications or divisions, for every N of at least 2, even if linear operations are free. Whether the ceiling is applied before or after the division is not fixed. Lean checks division-free polynomial identities and depends on two theorems that link the arithmetic model to Omega. The lower bound for circuits that allow division has not been formalized in Lean.

This is not a claim that Nvidia GPUs run faster tomorrow. Nvidia's GEMM documentation is cited for the point that real performance depends on hardware, reuse, and keeping thread blocks busy, not only on the asymptotic exponent. Any claim of cheaper training or inference is said to wait until algorithms are compared with CUDA at production sizes and precisions. A separate exact formula for rectangular multiplication is said to pin a dual exponent at 0.5, so an N by N matrix times an N by the ceiling of N to the power T stays at exponent two for T up to 0.5. The rectangular dimensions are compressed in the wording. No independent expert is described as having peer reviewed the 111-page lower bound. The proof is said to have gone straight into a GitHub repository that now holds 730 "unreferred" items. On 7 October, OpenAI withdrew three manuscripts and revised 14 others after a sign error in an algebraic-geometry paper. Those were not the matrix-multiplication papers. A readme warns that some unformalized results could have an issue. Whether a flood of machine-written papers stalls peer review is left as the open question.

Key points

  • OpenAI has proposed a matrix-multiplication exponent of 9/4, also stated as bounds of 2.25.
  • A 111-page manuscript went on GitHub on Tuesday. Its spoken title, "nine false," is garbled.
  • The problem is ranked 31 on Proof Atlas's top 500 and called arguably second only to P versus NP. Omega has been hunted for 57 years.
  • Strassen beat exponent three in 1969. A 2.522 figure in 1981 is tied to Schönhage in a broken sentence. Coppersmith and Winograd in 1990 have no number. Only 0.005 is said to have come off over the next 36 years, including Alpha Evolve.
  • Sebastian Bubeck says he did not expect to see the result. An internal OpenAI model is credited with the work. The upper bound is worded both over the complex numbers and over arbitrary fields.
  • LMU Munich researchers named Mahmoud Levent Dogan, Vladimir Lisikov, Kea Sakabe, and Michael Walter wrote an exposition of the October upper bound, with a Lean formalization.
  • The lower bound is not fully formalized for circuits that allow division. It is not a claim that Nvidia GPUs are faster tomorrow.
  • No independent peer review is described. On 7 October, three other manuscripts were withdrawn and 14 revised after a sign error. A readme warns that some unformalized results could have an issue.

item.title: The FCC has conditionally cleared SpaceX for up to a million orbital compute satellites
item.description:
The US Federal Communications Commission has given SpaceX a conditional approval to deploy up to 1 million satellites meant to process data in orbit. The grant is dated Wednesday, and called a first of its kind. One account says the systems are Starlink constellations and that the authorization is for 1 million satellites, so server capacity can move off a planet whose power grids are straining under AI. Another calls the constellation Star Mind, also Star-Mine and Star mine, and says the United States government has given Elon Musk permission to take the servers off the planet. The modules would use solar power to process data for use back on Earth, aimed at demand for AI and what is called super intelligence computing.

FCC chairman Brendan Carr called the move a "bold new frontier" for American leadership under President Donald Trump. He wrote that Star Mind and competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead in super intelligence. The commission's own framing is rendered as bringing humanity closer to a "Kardashev to civilization" able to harness the full power of the sun. That phrase is garbled and does not name a Kardashev type. Musk replied, "much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

SpaceX is cleared to build the network under the FCC's orbital-debris rules. Satellites would use optical links between them, plus radio in the 18.8 to 19.3 GHz downlink and the 28.6 to 29.1 GHz uplink. Radio would also carry backup and emergency telemetry, tracking, and command. SpaceX says a factory in Bastrop, Texas, could start producing the satellites as early as late 2027. Milestones require the first orbital data center by 25 November 2033, 100,000 satellites by 2035, and the full 1 million by 2040. The other account calls 2033 a target for the first center and full deployment a 2040 date, and it does not give 25 November, 100,000 satellites, or 2035. The FCC is already reviewing other firms' orbital data-center proposals and intends to process them quickly. Amazon's Kuiper unit and other rivals had argued that a million satellites could take centuries. Carr is said to have brushed that criticism off in March, with no year given.

The American Astronomical Society opposed the approval. It warned that a million-satellite shell would disrupt night-sky observations, create radio interference, raise collision risk, and add atmospheric pollution from launches and from satellites burning up on reentry. Putting a million compute modules in orbit by 2040 is called roughly 100 times as many satellites as exist now, and no current count is given. Keeping a million high-powered nodes running is called a logistical nightmare even if Starship flew every day. That daily flight rate is a premise, not a stated schedule. A line that chips probably degrade quickly under space radiation, and cannot simply be swapped, is hedged and cut off. The outlet's own view is that the unsolved problem is heat, because a vacuum has no air or water to cool a dense chip and heat has to leave through fragile panels, and that a million-satellite license now is less about imminent orbital data centers than about locking spectrum and orbital slots for American companies. That last sentence is unfinished.

Key points

  • The FCC has conditionally approved up to 1 million SpaceX satellites for orbital computing. The grant is dated Wednesday and called a first of its kind.
  • The constellation is called Starlink in one account and Star Mind, Star-Mine, and Star mine in the other.
  • Brendan Carr tied the decision to American leadership under Donald Trump. Musk said it will be a great asset to America and the world.
  • Links are optical between satellites, with radio at 18.8 to 19.3 GHz down and 28.6 to 29.1 GHz up.
  • A Bastrop, Texas, factory could start production as early as late 2027.
  • Milestones are a first orbital data center on 25 November 2033, 100,000 satellites by 2035, and 1 million by 2040. Another account gives only a 2033 target and full deployment by 2040.
  • Amazon's Kuiper unit had said a million satellites could take centuries. The American Astronomical Society warned of damage to observations, radio, collisions, and the atmosphere.
  • Heat in a vacuum, and a reading of the license as a grab for spectrum and orbital slots, are the outlet's view. A chip-radiation line is cut off.

item.title: Perplexity prices dated web snapshots at 5 dollars per 1,000 searches
item.description:
Perplexity Time Machine is live inside the Perplexity Search and Context APIs. Chief executive Aravind Srinivas, also spelled Arvind Srinivas, announced it on 25 November on X. He is quoted saying the tool shows a model of the web exactly as it was on any chosen date. Developers can post-train agents to predict events going back up to 365 days at launch, because a forecasting test is otherwise easy to cheat by looking up what already happened. Each crawler visit saves a dated copy and builds a version history for every link. A developer passes a timestamp with a time zone. Search returns only pages published or crawled by that cutoff. If an article was updated later, Time Machine is said to stop at the older saved version and keep the original title, date, and snippet. That "stops it" wording does not fully fix the retrieval rule. The same timestamp on the Context API lets a model read the archived full text, without the live web, and returns nothing if no copy existed then.

One account says users can post-train agents and predict the future, and that they gain what it calls advanced temporal modeling. It places the product in a race alongside startups "like XAI." The other account names rivals Epochal and Exa, and also an "X.AI startup Epochal," without making clear whether X.AI and Epochal are the same entity. Perplexity is said to have used reinforcement learning to train a model rendered GLM 5.3 flash on "resolve 2026" political questions from PolyMarket. Before that training, the scores were 0.94 on the live web and 0.77 with Time Machine, against PolyMarket's own odds of 0.79. A later line says an internal test scored 0.80 against those odds of 0.79. About 90 percent of live-web training groups taught the model nothing, because it found the answers immediately. Against Exa, on three sets of 1,000 queries covering random topics, news, and prediction markets, Time Machine returned publication dates on 98.8 to 99.5 percent of pages, against Exa's 66.1 to 77.7 percent. In the random test, 0.25 percent of Time Machine pages, across 18 queries, leaked future information. The Exa leak rate, across 62 queries, is missing from the sentence.

Perplexity is said to have crossed 1 billion dollars in annual run rate this November, and to be moving from consumer search into developer infrastructure. Time Machine is bundled into the existing APIs with no extra setup and no surcharge, at 5 dollars per 1,000 search requests and 1 dollar per 1,000 context URL fetches. A later line says 5 dollars "a pop." The offer is said to undercut Epochal before that startup opens to the public, and 365 days is called a fraction of a 30-year archive attributed to Epochal. The comparison to Epochal breaks off. The outlet's judgment is that beating market odds of 0.79 with a score of 0.80 is a one-point edge, not proof that agents are about to own Wall Street, and that freezing the search API does not erase 2025 or early 2026 news already sitting in a model's weights. It also says Perplexity is archiving permanent dated snapshots and selling that history, and that media lawyers will have something to say about it. Whose sites those snapshots are is not specified.

Key points

  • Perplexity Time Machine is live in the Search and Context APIs. Aravind Srinivas, also Arvind, announced it on 25 November on X.
  • Developers can lock a model to a past date, up to 365 days back, and each crawl keeps a dated copy.
  • A score before training was 0.94 on the live web and 0.77 with Time Machine, against PolyMarket odds of 0.79. A later internal figure is 0.80.
  • The model trained for that test is rendered GLM 5.3 flash, on questions rendered "resolve 2026" from PolyMarket.
  • On date coverage, Time Machine hit 98.8 to 99.5 percent of pages against Exa's 66.1 to 77.7 percent. A future-leak rate for Exa is missing.
  • The price is 5 dollars per 1,000 searches and 1 dollar per 1,000 context fetches. Perplexity is said to have crossed 1 billion dollars in annual run rate this November.
  • The account says the offer undercuts Epochal, and that a one-point edge over market odds is not proof agents will own markets.

item.title: Epochal says it can replay 30 years of the web, funded with 100 million dollars
item.description:
Epochal is described as raising 100 million dollars to build a historical web archive and replay 30 years of the web, including a plan to archive more than a trillion pages. The spoken account names three former members of Elon Musk's xAI founding team, Guo Dong Zhang, Zhi Hang Dai, and Manuel Kroiss, and says they are betting 100 billion dollars on a different problem: models that can explain a crash, a failure, or a leak after the fact, and that fall apart when asked to call the outcome beforehand. It then says Epochal launched on 24 November, with no year, and is funded with 100 million dollars of Zhang's own money. Bloomberg is cited for the point that no outside venture investors are named. The company is said to have assembled people from SpaceX, xAI, Ramp, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind. A quoted thesis says superhuman prediction will redefine almost every industry, because every decision is a prediction.

The first product, Time Portal, was built in 90 days. It is described as a time-gated environment of more than one trillion web pages and seven trillion URLs across more than 30 years, with minute-level timestamps on sites that update often. The written account says the trillion pages are still a plan. The spoken account describes them as already in Time Portal. An agent sits in a matching Linux sandbox so it does not know it is in a simulation: the clock, the operating system, the libraries, and the packet sources are rolled back to the chosen date, and web requests are kept on the time-gated path. Two of those sentences are cut off. Developers can test a limited version through Epochal's search, fetch, and sandbox APIs and SDKs.

Epochal ran agents on 347 live questions from Prediction Markets, Kalshi, and Polymarket, then replayed those questions weeks later through Time Portal. It is unclear whether "Prediction Markets" is a third source or a label for the other two. The correlation between the original forecast errors and the replayed ones is 0.98, against 0.16 for agents who had the live web after the event was resolved, and 0.49 for agents with no web access. The words after 0.98 are incomplete. The reading offered of 0.98 is that the simulator does not leak the future, and that this has not shown the system is any better at predicting tomorrow. Cutting off the live web cannot remove historical outcomes a model already absorbed in pre-training. Epochal has not said how the archive was assembled, or what licenses covered the pages. Selling three decades of scraped web as an API is described as an invitation to publishers, in a season of copyright lawsuits.

Epochal is placed in a wider departure from Musk's AI companies. After a February 2026 merger of xAI with SpaceX, every original xAI co-founder is said to have left. Egor Babushkin is said to have raised 1.1 billion dollars for River AI in August of this year. The commercial target is verifiable forecasting for banks, hedge funds, and supply chains, so a forecast can be graded against what happened and the model retrained. A stumble from "retain" to "retrain," and a phrase "8,000 of times," does not establish a count.

Key points

  • Epochal is described as raising 100 million dollars to replay about 30 years of the web. The founders are also said to be betting 100 billion dollars.
  • The named founders are Guo Dong Zhang, Zhi Hang Dai, and Manuel Kroiss, former members of xAI's founding team. The 100 million dollars is described as Zhang's own money, with no outside investors named, citing Bloomberg.
  • Launch is given as 24 November, with no year. People are said to have come from SpaceX, xAI, Ramp, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind.
  • Time Portal, built in 90 days, is described as more than one trillion pages and seven trillion URLs, inside a Linux sandbox with the clock rolled back.
  • On 347 questions from Prediction Markets, Kalshi, and Polymarket, replayed forecast errors correlated at 0.98, against 0.16 with the live web after the fact and 0.49 with no web.
  • That 0.98 is read as evidence the simulator does not leak, not as evidence of better forecasts. How the archive was licensed is not said.
  • After the February 2026 xAI-SpaceX merger, every original xAI co-founder is said to have left. Egor Babushkin is said to have raised 1.1 billion dollars for River AI in August.

item.title: A 10,000 crore rupee data-center project is tied to 400 direct jobs as a tax break runs to 2047
item.description:
Antara Gupta hosted Osama Manzar, Amit Chaurasia, and Gaurav Shinh on whether India's data-center boom is for the country's own digital future or a lease of land, power, and water to global technology companies. Manzar is founder and director of the Digital Empowerment Foundation. Chaurasia is founder and chief executive of Dataneers, described as building storage and cloud systems. Shinh is founder of SciKiq in one introduction and founder and chief executive of SciKiq in the other. Gupta cited Crisil for a five-fold jump in India's data-center capacity, to 7.5 gigawatts by 2030, drawing more than 3 lakh crore rupees. She also said Crisil puts three-quarters of an upcoming 6 gigawatts in Visakhapatnam, Mumbai, and Hyderabad. Shinh referred to a figure he called "1 uh five" before returning to the 7.5 gigawatts. She said residents in Thane are protesting a 420-megawatt AWS facility next to their homes, later called a "420 megawatt AWS side," over the risk of power cuts. Citizen groups in Visakhapatnam are questioning a 20-year water guarantee for a Google-Adani project she called "15 billion," with no currency, in a city she said already has a daily water deficit.

CtrlS, she said, has signed a 10,000 crore rupee deal in Bihar projected to create 400 direct jobs. She later said the commitment is a 150-megawatt center, that she believes the site is 100 acres, and that only 100 of the 400 jobs are on site. The 100 acres is her belief, not a confirmed area. Manzar treated the jobs line as already answering the question. He said data taken without consent, and land and water that belong to the community, are being given away on promise, and that the people asking are mostly outsiders seeking profit. Nothing, he said, should move without consent. Shinh said he was not speaking for the government, that companies are there because government gave permission, and that renting racks to Amazon, AWS, or Google, with the model free to sit anywhere, is not value capture. He wants India self-sufficient in the infrastructure, and he wants the argument kept neutral between competitors. Chaurasia said both views hold in their own frame. He said the power sector is now distributed enough for small capacity additions, that states have to offer tax benefits because the return on capital is probably three, four, or five years out, and that the cities lead because the talent is there. He credited Mumbai's older business role, Chandrababu Naidu and the Andhra government, and Bangalore, and he would rather see centers spread across India.

Pressed on households and farms, Manzar said a line that "70 percent of all the planned data centers are already said no to us," after an election in which Democrats gained seats. That sentence is garbled and does not establish a country or a count. He said mega centers serve a compulsion to archive what he called garbage on social media, and that the constant energy they need is not sustainable. He expects a shift to small, local models. Shinh said centers also serve cars, which he rendered "lactic," healthcare and "teley medicine," robotics, aerospace, and manufacturing, and he asked whether India would accept the same centers sitting in China, Peru, or the United States. He favors treating water and using it more carefully, not only opposing the plants. Chaurasia called the resource problem global, said people whose land is taken should share the value rather than remain salaried labor, and said opposition should be separated from a habit of opposing projects such as the bullet train and Vande Bharat. Manzar rejected a return-to-the-bullock-cart framing. He said Bangalore still takes him 30 minutes to drive 3 kilometers, that more than half of Indians do not use the internet after 30 years of it, since 1995, and that calling those people backward is arrogance. A data center, he said, is useful only if it serves that larger population, and he does not see the projects doing so.

On Union Budget 2026-27, Gupta said eligible foreign cloud providers were given a tax holiday until 2047 if they use Indian data centers. She called it both a 21-year break and a two-decade break. A claim that Indian rentals are already 30 to 35 percent cheaper, and that the beneficiary is "say a trillion dollar" company, is her supposition. Shinh said the hyperscalers would have come anyway, and he opposes the holiday if it kills people building infrastructure in India. He said GPU time in India is already far cheaper, and that India has the cheapest telecom plans. Gupta said Crisil projects hyperscalers will control 75 to 80 percent of India's "lease" data-center capacity by 2030. "Lease" may be a garbled "leased." Chaurasia said he completely disagrees with tax holidays for hyperscalers. He said 25 or 26 years of India's technology story were application work for foreign firms, and he recalled a student in Pune last year being told that a software superpower is a myth. He said almost 100 percent of data-center technology, the operating system, the network gear, and the storage, will be imported, and he compared the pattern to the East India Company. Manzar said the holiday spends taxpayers' resources, that India can build the centers and import only what it must, and that real-time service to people does not require one central hall. He recalled 1995, when mail to a neighbor was routed through the United States.

In a round where each guest defended an assigned position, Manzar argued for pausing new centers until a project can show better digital access, real local jobs, and a measurable gain for the host community, because the data is people's data. Shinh asked who speaks for a population he put at 1.4 billion, and said a street protest is not a vote of the whole country. Manzar said elected members and civil-society groups are the representatives, and that people come onto the street when they are not heard. Chaurasia said the claim that about half the country does not use the internet is factually wrong, in a sentence that also garbles who redefined that half as people without a meaningful connection. He cited TRAI for nearly 78 percent of Indians on mobile or other internet, and said UPI is used by only 25 percent, a figure he joined to "rural India" and to a rural population of 980 million, so the base of the 25 percent is not clear. He said UPI has surpassed Mastercard and Visa, and that India has started exporting payment-gateway technology. On a copper smelter in Tamil Nadu, spoken as a "co copper" plant and planned by Sterlite Industries, he said a protest stopped the factory and India is now a net copper importer. His population figure was "1.4 4 billion."

Defending priority power and water for data centers, Chaurasia said a car is now electronics and software, and that a fridge, a phone, and a gas line already throw off data, so the centers have to be widespread. Manzar called a great deal of technological development anti-human, and said a digital-only rule for a pension took three decades to reach a 50-year-old in a village. He also objected to an attendance app made mandatory for workers he called "narga" and "ng." Chaurasia answered with a 1980s prime minister's line that only 10 or 15 paise of every budgeted rupee reached the poor, and with direct benefit transfer, Aadhaar, and a vaccination app he called "co." Shinh said a Western template does not fit India, and he asked which sector loses electricity today. Chaurasia's example of chip costs and data-transfer costs falling 50 to 60 percent is a hypothetical, not a reported result. Shinh said those gains are 10 to 15 years away, while the megawatts have to be paid for now.

Asked to defend welcoming global hyperscalers even if Indian cloud companies lose, Shinh said that is the opposite of his own view, that markets should decide, and that he would subsidize neither foreign hyperscalers nor local firms that do not innovate. A buyer spending 5 dollars, or 5 rupees, should look at the return. Chaurasia said there is still no level field against hyperscalers flush with cash, while Indian deep-technology companies cannot find patient capital. He said engineering centers in Bangalore, Pune, Hyderabad, Mumbai, and a place he called "Gura" are run by foreign companies. "Gura" is not resolved. Shinh said the fair comparison is AWS and Google with Adani and Ambani, rendered "andan adanis and ammanis," not with small "mom and shop pop" centers. Manzar said about 50 years of capitalism has been creating oligarchs, that micro, small, and medium enterprises are 85 percent of nano and micro entrepreneurs, and that the centers were agreed with government while people were bypassed. Shinh said a decentralized center is a good theory he has not seen work unless small sites can feed a larger grid. The closest case he offered is China, where data generated on one coast is processed on another, spoken as "other post," near the resources. He wants an Indian template rather than a copy. Gupta closed on a question neither side answered: whether India is building a foundation for Indian AI, or giving away too much land, power, and tax revenue.

Key points

  • Antara Gupta spoke with Osama Manzar of the Digital Empowerment Foundation, Amit Chaurasia of Dataneers, and Gaurav Shinh of SciKiq.
  • Crisil is cited for 7.5 gigawatts by 2030 and more than 3 lakh crore rupees, and also for three-quarters of an upcoming 6 gigawatts in Visakhapatnam, Mumbai, and Hyderabad.
  • Thane residents are protesting a 420-megawatt AWS site. Visakhapatnam's water objection is tied to a Google-Adani project called "15 billion," with no currency.
  • CtrlS is tied to 10,000 crore rupees in Bihar, 400 direct jobs, and a later line of 150 megawatts with 100 jobs on site. The 100 acres is the host's "I believe."
  • Manzar wants community consent. Shinh says renting space to Amazon or Google is not value capture. Chaurasia says talent and a three-to-five-year payback explain why the big cities lead.
  • A tax holiday for eligible foreign cloud providers runs until 2047. Shinh and Chaurasia oppose it. Crisil is cited for hyperscalers holding 75 to 80 percent of "lease" capacity by 2030.
  • Internet use is more than half offline in Manzar's account and nearly 78 percent online in Chaurasia's TRAI citation. A 25 percent UPI figure is tied unclearly to 980 million rural residents.
  • Chip-cost cuts of 50 to 60 percent are a hypothetical. "Gura," "1.4 4 billion," and a 70 percent refusal tied to Democrats are unresolved wordings.

item.title: Oracle says Google's AI chips arrive on its cloud in 2027
item.description:
Google's tensor processing units are coming to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in 2027. Amit Raja Naik spoke with Christopher G. Chelliah, also called Chris Chelliah, senior vice president for technology and customer strategy in JAPAC at Oracle, at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas. The conversation is placed both "just last month" and on the third day of the event, with the chip news called "yesterday." No event date is established. Oracle already runs its database services on Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. Starting in 2027 the Google partnership is described as running both ways, and Oracle Cloud is described as set to become the first hyperscale cloud outside Google to offer Google's TPUs, alongside GPUs, for training and running models. That "first" is the framing of the account. Chelliah does not say it. A line that Oracle "bought" its database into the cloud is not confirmed as a purchase.

Chelliah said customers have moved past experiments and want business outcomes, without walled gardens of context. AI, he said, needs data that is available, and inference depends on the chip. Oracle's multicloud lesson was to make the same data available in every cloud. Uptake, he said, was phenomenal, and the company is opening the same kind of choice for AI. Asked whether the saving is the accelerator or the fact that data does not have to move, he said both. Data has piled up for decades and is scattered, and an AI result has to be grounded in it. He also said customers want a choice of inference chips because that is how they get price performance. He gave no count, cost, or test duration for moving a workload from GPUs to TPUs. Most customers, he said, already have a test harness and a router that picks a model to save tokens. Oracle would let them keep that harness, bring their own model, and run each model on the chip where it does better. He said the company already helps people compare chips, through always-free Oracle Cloud accounts, starter credits, and the ability to flip models and chips without other changes. A caption line, "they're going at that minute gravity," is unclear.

Naik said there are close to 75 agents already built, and about 25 Fusion Cloud applications. Chelliah did not repeat either number. He said Fusion and industry applications can deliver an outcome out of the box: hospitality, healthcare, and a manufacturing supply chain were his examples. An outcome is set in English, and the agents work in the background. Oracle ships those agents and the toolkit, so a customer can extend them or build their own. An AI data platform, he said, can reach enterprise data on premises, on Oracle's cloud, or on the other hyperscale clouds. On security, he said protection has to sit in what he called the atomic layer, not get wrapped on at the end. Over the coming years the largest new flow of data will be machines and agents, not people, so identity, access, governance, and provenance have to travel with every step. His example is a banking agent that holds a micro-credential, also called a subcredential, allowing an inquiry but not a transaction. He said that pattern holds on Oracle's cloud and in the multicloud setup.

Naik said Google reports up to 80 percent better performance per dollar for low-latency serving, and asked how much of that customers should expect when the TPUs arrive in 2027. Chelliah did not confirm 80 percent or any share of it. He said every model has its own token and performance shape, and compared a car, a bus, and a truck: each gets there, and the right one depends on the question. Naik also raised a Cerebras partnership and Nvidia's position, and asked whether other clouds' chips would be offered the same way. Chelliah did not name Cerebras or Nvidia and did not confirm those chips. He said Oracle removes barriers to adoption, has been taking technology to customers for almost five decades, and will keep adding to the platform. He did not say whether aligning rival platforms or the people behind them is harder. He called the relationship co-opetition, and said customers should not have to change what he called their "religion" to reach an outcome. His advice to CIOs and CISOs is to start from wherever the company already is: ready-made agents inside applications, trusted use of data it already holds, or the best price for inference. Banking, manufacturing, hospitality, and retail, he said, are covered by hundreds if not thousands of use cases. Oracle, he said, can take an outcome a customer wants and show it working in one to two weeks.

Key points

  • Google TPUs are coming to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in 2027. Christopher G. Chelliah, also Chris Chelliah, described the partnership at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas.
  • Amit Raja Naik conducted the interview. The timing is both "last month" and the third day of the event.
  • Oracle already runs database services on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. OCI is described as set to be the first hyperscale cloud outside Google to offer the TPUs. Chelliah does not say "first."
  • He said the gain is both the chip and not having to move data, and he gave no cost or test time for a GPU-to-TPU switch.
  • Close to 75 agents and about 25 Fusion applications are Naik's figures. Chelliah did not restate them.
  • Security, he said, belongs in the atomic layer, with short-lived identity. A banking micro-credential could allow an inquiry and block a transaction.
  • Up to 80 percent better performance per dollar is Naik's citation of Google. Chelliah did not adopt it. Cerebras and Nvidia are likewise unconfirmed by him.
  • His advice is to start from the company's current AI use. He said a customer outcome can be shown working in one to two weeks.

item.title: India warned the UN on terrorist misuse of AI, alongside seven other developments
item.description:
India has warned the United Nations that terrorists could misuse AI, and has urged human oversight, stronger cybersecurity, and a greater role for developing countries in writing the rules. The same list says Skyroot's Raman-2 engine cleared its acceptance test for Vikram-1's second flight, and that GalaxEye ordered electric propulsion from Bellatrix for 30 Drishti Gen-II satellites, also described as a business-to-business order. Karnataka approved Pixxel's GigaPixxel satellite factory. Indian AI startups raised $1.6 billion in the first nine months of 2026, according to Tracxn, with funding up 96 percent and startup deals plunging. Anthropic's Siren test asks whether AI agents misuse files and credentials, and is also described as a trap set for those agents. Microsoft called an internal Code Red after a major outage, with the question of why recovery took so long left as the subject rather than an answer. Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 US counts.

Those are the claims as listed. The figures and names above are the ones that list states, and it does not add a further count, date, or quotation.

Key points

  • India warned the UN that terrorists could misuse AI, and urged human oversight, stronger cybersecurity, and a larger role for developing countries.
  • The list says Raman-2 cleared its test for Vikram-1's second flight, GalaxEye ordered Bellatrix propulsion for 30 Drishti Gen-II satellites, and Karnataka approved Pixxel's GigaPixxel factory.
  • It says Indian AI startups raised $1.6 billion in the first nine months of 2026, according to Tracxn, with funding up 96 percent and deals plunging.
  • It names Anthropic's Siren test, Microsoft's Code Red, and Huawei's conviction on 10 of 12 counts, without adding counts or dates beyond that.

item.title: Anupam Sidhant says a century of artists will not roll over for AI
item.description:
Anupam Sidhant, co-founder of Bombay Locale, pushes back on daily claims that design, story, cinema, and music are dead. In the exchange those claims are placed on Twitter, as a funeral a day. He asks why a good technology product would mean artists simply quit. The written line says artists who have lasted a century will not roll over. The spoken line says artists who have been around for the last 100 years, and been through everything, will not roll over and ask what their work is for. He says the narrative around AI is terrible, and that AI has one chance to fix it, because the technology is essentially good. The spoken sentence breaks off at "essentially a good." He compares that chance with Web 3 crypto, which had one chance, then uses an unfinished "They it up," after which he says nobody talks about crypto anymore. He says India had that kind of movement, and that AI has it now, and he asks whether stories can make the narrative better.

Key points

  • Anupam Sidhant, co-founder of Bombay Locale, rejects daily claims that design, story, cinema, and music are dead.
  • He says artists who have lasted a century, also "the last 100 years," will not give up their work because a technology product arrived.
  • He says AI has one chance to fix a terrible narrative, and that the technology is essentially good. The spoken sentence breaks off.
  • Web 3 crypto is his comparison for a chance that was missed. "They it up" does not say what was done with that chance.

item.title: Anupam Sidhant tells filmmakers to ask whether a task needs AI at all
item.description:
Anupam Sidhant, co-founder of Bombay Locale and described as an IIT Bombay alumnus, was asked how he answers filmmakers who say AI is shortchanging the craft and that critical thinking is leaving the room. The questioner called him a pedigree of IIT Bombay. Sidhant said there is some truth in that complaint, including inside his own team. A common warning, which he calls fair, is that people should not let AI do their thinking. He said the overall IQ of the world is going to dumb down because of that, and that this is certain. He looks at the work of people who are 18 and 19 and asks them, each time they use AI, whether the task needed it. He asks himself the same question. Many tasks, he said, do not. Some of that use makes his own process more annoying rather than faster. The sentence is garbled at "we just happen," so what exactly becomes annoying is the use, not a second claim. A question about whether he wanted his IIT Bombay background as an edge is not answered in the exchange. The co-founder title and the surname Sidhant come from the report's identification of him. The exchange itself addresses him as Anupam.

Key points

  • Anupam Sidhant, identified as co-founder of Bombay Locale and an IIT Bombay alumnus, was asked about AI shortchanging filmmaking.
  • He said there is some truth in that, including on his own team.
  • He calls it fair that people should not let AI do their thinking, and he said the world's IQ will dumb down because of it.
  • He asks 18- and 19-year-olds, and himself, whether a task even needs AI. Many tasks, he said, do not.
  • Some of that use makes his process more annoying. His answer on using an IIT background as an edge is not in the exchange.

item.title: Bombay Locale's co-founder expects AI to cost jobs and says people are cheaper in India
item.description:
Anupam Sidhant, co-founder of Bombay Locale, is the person named on this exchange. The exchange itself does not attach each line to a name. Asked whether this leads to a loss of jobs, one speaker says "Of course it will," because the models will change and the work will change, and compares it to an e-rickshaw arriving and the hand rickshaw going. Another speaker agrees. The same stretch says the creative opportunity, or the creative ability, is not going to shrink, worded in the written account as the creative ability of people. A speaker wants to empower "my 10 HODs with AI," and the sentence breaks off, then calls the problem specific to India. "HOD" is not expanded. Another line, "But it is indelicate," is unclear. People, the exchange agrees, are cheaper than AI. "We throw 10 people at a problem. We don't throw AI." In a country like the United States, a western country, the exchange says they will use AI to minimize things. "In India, you can't."

Key points

  • The report names Anupam Sidhant, co-founder of Bombay Locale. The exchange does not label which lines are his.
  • Jobs will be lost as the models and the work change. The comparison is an e-rickshaw replacing a hand rickshaw.
  • Creative ability is said not to shrink.
  • A wish to empower "10 HODs" with AI is cut off.
  • People are cheaper than AI. The line is that India throws 10 people at a problem, while a western country uses AI to minimize things.

item.title: Anupam Sidhant tells film students to pick a tool and get the story out
item.description:
Anupam Sidhant, co-founder of Bombay Locale, was asked what he tells a film student. The exchange addresses him as Anupam. He said cinema has always been problem solving and nothing else. Students should use whatever tool they have, pick the one they want, and get the story out. That, he said, is the only way to make films. It has always been the same, and nobody will ever hand them a chance. He told them not to listen to the old folks or to anyone, not to be idealistic, not to be a puritan, and not to be a Luddite. A garbled stretch says Werner Herzog will teach documentaries his own way, that the speaker loves Herzog and loves Del Toro, and that students should not listen to him. The day a student can afford it, he said, they can be like Tarantino and refuse a technology. Until then they should not reject anything. The sentence ends unfinished at "that's going to hurt."

Another speaker called the remarks a summary of the whole discussion. A later turn, whose speaker is not named, ties the point to early friends at TVF. When those videos were being made, everybody looked at the makers as if they were stupid and asked why anyone would watch, and the present argument sounds the same. The written account says few believed the videos would find an audience, and it attributes that memory to Sidhant. The spoken line says everybody treated the makers as stupid. Neither line states a job title at TVF.

Key points

  • Anupam Sidhant tells film students that cinema has always been problem solving, and that they should pick a tool and get the story out.
  • He says not to be a puritan or a Luddite, and not to reject a technology until they can afford to, a position he ties to Tarantino.
  • Werner Herzog and Del Toro are named. The sentence joining them to "don't listen" is garbled.
  • Early TVF videos are the comparison: everybody is said to have asked why anyone would watch. A written line says few believed they would find an audience.
